content: Visceral fat, also referred to as inner organ fat, is located within the peritoneal cavity and is situated between internal organs. This is distinct from subcutaneous fat, which is found beneath the skin, and intramuscular fat, which is distributed within skeletal muscle tissue. An excessive accumulation of visceral fat results in a characteristic pot belly or beer belly appearance, where the abdomen protrudes significantly. This body type is often described as apple-shaped, in contrast to the pear-shaped body type, where fat is predominantly stored around the hips and buttocks. Visceral fat consists of several adipose tissue depots, including mesenteric fat, epididymal white adipose tissue (EWAT), and perirenal fat depots. The accumulation of visceral fat is strongly associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Visceral fat can be measured or estimated using various methods. These include manual assessment, bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) diagnostic machines, or imaging techniques such as computed tomography (CT) scans performed at the level of the umbilicus. When using BIA, visceral fat area (VFA) can be calculated using the formula: VFA = a₀ + a₁(V₀'Wc), where a₀ and a₁ are constants, V₀' represents the voltage measured at the flank, and Wc is the waist circumference. The voltage measured at the flank increases as visceral fat levels rise. This is because the resistance of intra-abdominal fat is higher than that of fat-free mass, leading to variations in visceral fat even among individuals with the same waist circumference. Visceral fat is associated with a greater number of risk factor syndromes compared to body mass index (BMI), which is calculated by dividing body weight by the square of height. This highlights the importance of visceral fat as a more specific indicator of metabolic and cardiovascular health risks than BMI alone.
